## My thinking

I have about 12 mu of contracted land in the village. Same fields my family has worked for thirty years. My knees are not what they were, and my youngest son works in the city — he comes back at harvest to help run the machines, but the day-to-day is on me.

Wheat and corn. That is what I grow. That is what my father grew on this land, and that is what the grain station will buy from me without argument. I know exactly when to sow, how much water to put down, what the stalks should look like in April. I am not going to risk my income at 64 on vegetables or something I have never grown. My neighbor tried growing garlic a few years ago and lost money when prices collapsed. Wheat and corn are stable. The government still subsidizes grain and I get a direct payment per mu.

In October I will sow winter wheat on all 12 mu. I use the improved variety from the county seed station — not hybrid, but better than the old seed. I will ask my nephew to bring his rotary tiller. I put down base fertilizer before sowing, then top-dress urea at jointing. Three irrigations: pre-sowing, jointing, and heading. Two sprays — one herbicide in winter, one fungicide when rust comes in spring.

After wheat harvest in June, I will call the machinery service to direct-seed corn into the stubble without tillage. No point tilling twice. I buy hybrid corn seed every year, same brand I have used for ten years. Corn gets one irrigation at sowing if the ground is dry — summer rains usually handle the rest. One herbicide spray after emergence.

I keep enough wheat for household flour. Everything else I sell.
